title: Linear and binary search
summary: Halve a sorted range until the target is found, and get the boundaries exactly right.

steps.title: Halve the range each step
body: Linear search checks items one by one: `O(n)`. If the array is **sorted** you can do far better.
Look at the middle item. If the target is bigger, it can only be in the right half; if smaller, the left half. Throw the other half away and repeat. That is **binary search**: `O(log n)`.
Watch `lo`, `hi` and `mid` close in on 23. Ten items, found in three looks.

steps.prompt: This version prints every middle **value** it looks at. What does it print?
steps.explain: Range 0..8 gives mid 4 (value 5): too big. Range 0..3 gives mid 1 (value 2): too small. Range 2..3 gives mid 2 (value 3), then range 3..3 gives 4.
hints: Write down `lo` and `hi` after each look. `mid` rounds down.

steps.title: Off-by-one traps
body: Binary search is famous for being easy to get *almost* right. The rules that fit together:
- loop `while (lo <= hi)`: a range of one item (`lo == hi`) must still be checked.
- move **past** `mid`: `lo = mid + 1` or `hi = mid - 1`. `mid` is already checked.
- `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` instead of `(lo + hi) / 2`, which can overflow for huge arrays.
Change one rule without changing the others and the search either misses items or loops forever.

steps.prompt: A search uses `lo = mid` instead of `lo = mid + 1`. With `lo = 3`, `hi = 4` and the target bigger than `a[3]`, what happens?
options: `mid` is 3 again, `lo` stays 3: an infinite loop
It finds the target one step later
steps.explain: `mid = 3 + (4 - 3) / 2 = 3`, so `lo = mid` changes nothing. The range never shrinks.
Inclusive bounds, a `<=` loop, and moving past `mid` on both sides.

steps.title: Fix the search
prompt: This `BinarySearch` should return the index of `target` in the sorted array `a`, or `-1`. It has **two** bugs: it misses some items and can read past the end of the array.
Fix it so all the tests pass. Keep it a binary search.
template: Dojo.Eq($"finds {dojoA[dojoI]} at index {dojoI}", dojoI, BinarySearch(dojoA, dojoA[dojoI]));
Dojo.Eq("a missing middle value gives -1", -1, BinarySearch(dojoA, 6));
Dojo.Eq("a value bigger than all gives -1", -1, BinarySearch(dojoA, 100));
Dojo.Eq("a value smaller than all gives -1", -1, BinarySearch(dojoA, 0));
Dojo.Eq("an empty array gives -1", -1, BinarySearch(new int[0], 4));
Dojo.Eq("a single item is found", 0, BinarySearch(new[] { 4 }, 4));
hints: If `hi` starts at `a.Length`, it points one past the end. Either use exclusive bounds everywhere, or make it inclusive.

steps.prompt: Match each binary search mistake to its symptom.
pairs: the last remaining item is never checked

steps.title: Lower bound
prompt: Often you want *where a value would go*, not just whether it is present. Write `int LowerBound(int[] a, int target)`: the **first index** `i` with `a[i] >= target`, or `a.Length` if every item is smaller. `a` is sorted and may contain duplicates.
Use a half-open range: `lo = 0`, `hi = a.Length`, `while (lo < hi)`. If `a[mid] < target` the answer is right of `mid`; otherwise `mid` **might** be the answer, so `hi = mid`.
The tests run 200,000 searches on a million items: `O(log n)` each, please. No `Array.BinarySearch`.
template: Dojo.Eq("an empty array gives 0", 0, LowerBound(new int[0], 5));
for (var dojoI = 0; dojoI < dojoBig.Length; dojoI++) dojoBig[dojoI] = dojoI / 4 * 4;
for (var dojoQ = 0; dojoQ < 200_000; dojoQ++) dojoSum += LowerBound(dojoBig, dojoQ * 5);
Dojo.Eq("200,000 searches on a million items", 99_999_800_000L, dojoSum);
hints: Half-open range `[lo, hi)`: start with `hi = a.Length` and loop `while (lo < hi)`.
`if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid;` and return `lo` when they meet.
